items.why: The report states that D, G and 2D are detected on both metals, with "G 1580.3" and "2D 2680.9" on Au and "G 1580.9" and "2D 2695.6" on Cu, and it concludes that both layers are graphene.
It reports D near 1344–1348 cm-1, gives Au "D/G = 110.9/115.9 = 0.96" and Cu "D/G = 13/23 = 0.57 with about ±45% uncertainty", and says it "would not claim Cu is less defective than Au".
The report never gives the authors' hypothesis that rapid droplet solidification causes strain behind the stronger D on Au. Strain appears only in its discussion of the Cu 2D shift.

It checks strain against G and 2D positions ("Strain and doping shift G and 2D together... A pure-strain reading would need G to rise by about 7 cm-1") and treats D/G as a defect measure. However, it never says outright that D needs defects or edges to be activated, or that strain alone cannot produce D.

It asks "Which laser wavelength... This sets the L_D values and tests whether the 2D position is standard", and it notes the λ^4 dependence and that "The 2D position comparison is valid only if both spectra used the same laser".

It notes the Cu signal is "about 5x weaker and noisier" and that "Cu intensity ratios carry large uncertainty". It gives error bars on Cu widths and ratios and asks about acquisition time because "The Cu noise... limits the D and G detection".

wrong_claims.why: Although the wavelength is unknown, the report gives quantitative L_D values ("At 532 nm: L_D about 4.5 nm"; property L_D_nm "Au: about 4.5"; Cu "4.6-8"). It hedges them with an assumed 532 nm laser and a 488–633 nm range.
The report never attributes the Au D peak to strain; it lists strain_sign as "none determined".
